report.headline: Well & Truly Cheese & Jalapeño Thins: strong packaging and a loyal Southwark niche, but distribution gaps and price resistance cap wider demand
key_findings: Distribution is the dominant barrier: 90.8% of simulated agents reported no stocking store along their week, and all zero-conversion bottom boroughs (Kingston upon Thames, Richmond upon Thames, Kensington and Chelsea) cite no store nearby.

Southwark is the only proven pocket: 15 of 24 simulated purchases (20.8% conversion among 72 Southwark agents) came from there, driven by convenience stores on commute and home routes; this is simulated conversion, not evidence of real demand.

Price is the main friction among those who notice: 8 of 24 non-buyers (0.4% of all agents) rejected on price, with quotes consistently comparing £2.80 with a ~£1.80 norm; this is a small absolute count, so treat as directional.
Visibility is a secondary leak: 70 agents (3.5%) walked past without noticing, and 41 (2.0%) found it stocked where they live but not where they needed it, especially at work or after exercise.

Packaging salience (4/5) and the high-protein/gluten-free claims convert a specific niche — commuters, gym-goers and WFH high/mid-income shoppers in Southwark — but loyalty to existing brands and lack of need cap impulse switching.

rejection_reasons.title: No stocking store on the weekly route
rejection_reasons.detail: 90.8% of all simulated agents (1,815) never encountered the product because no store along their week stocked it. This is the single largest loss and explains zero conversion in Kingston upon Thames, Richmond upon Thames and Kensington and Chelsea, and near-zero in Greenwich (3.1%).

rejection_reasons.title: Price above the £1.80 snack norm
rejection_reasons.detail: 8 agents (0.4% of all) explicitly rejected at £2.80 versus a habitual ~£1.80, including low-income carers and students in Southwark and commuters passing through. The absolute count is small, so this is a directional signal rather than a proven mass barrier.

rejection_reasons.title: Not noticed on shelf
rejection_reasons.detail: 70 agents (3.5%) walked past a stocking store without registering the pack, despite a 4/5 packaging score. Quotes describe rushed commutes and non-scanning behaviour, suggesting the pack needs secondary placement or signage rather than a redesign.

rejection_reasons.title: Stocked at home, needed at work or gym
rejection_reasons.detail: 41 agents (2.0%) saw it near home but found no stock at the moment of need — at work, on the commute, or after exercise. This is a placement mismatch, not a product rejection.

rejection_reasons.title: No current need / loyal to existing brand
rejection_reasons.detail: 39 agents (1.9%) saw it but felt no need, and 3 (0.1%) stayed with their usual brand. Quotes cite already-sorted snack cupboards and habit; this is a trial-conversion problem best addressed with sampling or a first-purchase incentive.

interested_segments.title: Southwark convenience shoppers (home and commute)
interested_segments.detail: 72 agents, 22 interested, 15 bought (20.8% conversion). Purchases clustered at Tesco Express, Sainsbury's Local, Costcutter, Nisa, Londis and independent convenience stores on commute and home routes. This is the only segment with enough simulated purchases to justify scaling spend.

interested_segments.title: Health-motivated commuters passing through Southwark / London Bridge
interested_segments.detail: Quotes from commuters travelling to City of London, West End and Canary Wharf cite the protein and gluten-free claims and the jalapeño kick as the trigger. They buy when the pack is on their route (e.g. Little Waitrose, Best-one, Prezzemolo & Vitale) but will not detour.

interested_segments.title: Gym-goers and post-workout snackers in Southwark
interested_segments.detail: Several purchases followed a workout or a savoury craving, with high-protein cited as the reason. This segment is small in the simulation but shows repeat intent and low price sensitivity among high-income buyers.

interested_segments.title: Black and Greenwich segments (early signal only)
interested_segments.detail: Black ethnicity: 273 agents, 11 interested, 9 bought (3.3%); Greenwich: 64 agents, 2 bought (3.1%). Both are small-conversion signals dominated by no-store-nearby, so treat as watch-list rather than proven demand.

action_items.action: Deepen Southwark convenience distribution before expanding: prioritise Tesco Express, Sainsbury's Local, Costcutter, Nisa, Londis and independent stores on Southwark / London Bridge commute routes and near gyms.
action_items.rationale: Southwark delivered 15 of 24 simulated purchases at 20.8% conversion, while 90.8% of all agents cited no nearby stock. Fixing the proven pocket is higher-confidence than chasing zero-conversion boroughs.

action_items.action: Add a £2.50–£2.60 price-marked pack or a '2 for £5' mechanic in Southwark convenience stores, and test a smaller 60–70g pack at ~£1.80–£2.00.
action_items.rationale: Price rejections consistently compare £2.80 with a ~£1.80 norm; a closer entry price lowers the trial barrier without abandoning the premium protein positioning. The count is small, so run this as a controlled test rather than a national price cut.

action_items.action: Secure secondary placement at till points, lunchtime fixtures and gym-adjacent stores in Southwark, with shelf-talkers calling out 'high protein' and 'gluten free'.
action_items.rationale: 3.5% of agents walked past without noticing and 2.0% found it only where they live, not where they need it. Secondary siting addresses both the visibility leak and the need-moment mismatch.

action_items.action: Run in-store sampling and a first-purchase trial incentive at Southwark convenience stores on weekday mornings and post-work evenings.
action_items.rationale: 1.9% saw it but felt no need and 0.1% stayed loyal to existing brands; quotes describe habit and 'snacks already sorted'. Sampling converts the noticed-but-unconvinced group at the point of decision.

action_items.action: Do not fund broad out-of-borough distribution yet; monitor Greenwich and Black ethnicity segments as a watch-list, and revisit only if a Southwark-adjacent listing produces repeat sales.
action_items.rationale: Greenwich (3.1%) and Black ethnicity (3.3%) show early interest but are dominated by no-store-nearby and rest on small counts. Expanding now would repeat the distribution leak rather than build on proven demand.
